speaker: Li Lu
text: Sure.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The third one is about underperformance and how you keep yourself in business, even though you’re two years into it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: First of all, the value principle — I put it this way.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I think all intelligent investment is value investment, because you always want to get a little more than what you pay for.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What you pay is the price; what you get is value.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Whatever value you can express yourself, whether it is in a business that is stagnant or even declining but pays you a whole bunch of money back, or a company that is rapidly growing, or a bet that has only a small percentage of winning and a large percentage of losing, therefore you spread — all of that come down to your understanding of where value will be created.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The basic principle is discounted future cash flow, to the extent that you can understand and estimate it accurately.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They all come down to the same mathematics.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s why I say almost all intelligent investing is value investing.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The basic principle doesn’t change.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You can apply it differently based on where your circle of competence is, going back to the concept Warren articulated so well.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Energy is obviously essential, an essential layer of the economy.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I see energy and transportation, manufacturing, communication, and then knowledge-based services.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Those are essentially the entire economy.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Of course, they have applications in every single layer.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Of cause right now, the constraint on AI ranges from chips to electricity to labor.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It applies differently, and it has an impact on climate.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Any one of those subjects, we could go into almost endless aspects of it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But your third question, regarding your question about crypto, I have a very simple answer.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I don’t think anything of it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I think eventually it will disappear on its own, and that’s okay, because it’s fundamentally bogus.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you think about what constitutes a currency that is redeemable, it is enforced because of the forces associated with it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Without that mechanism of enforcement, you cannot have any enforceable measure of settlement or store of wealth.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Some guys creating it out of a garage doesn’t do the job.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Yes, it helps criminals and facilitates all kinds of illicit transactions.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I think we’re all better off banning it, but that’s okay.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If somebody wants to collect it in the same way people think a certain artist is worth a certain price, that’s your personal preference.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But as a society, I think nothing of it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s very simple.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Now, your question is very real.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You’re buying into it, but then, of course, you also want to ask it to cooperate with you.

speaker: Li Lu
text: As I said, that is where human psychology is.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Everybody likes to have the best of both worlds.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In fact, they want everything – I want to be doing win-win, but I also want to report good numbers every year at least, preferably every quarter, then every month, every day, every hour – Pretty soon, you will become a speculator.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You cannot have both worlds.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Either you think the market is there to instruct you, or you think the market is there to serve you.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You can only take one of the two.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Anyone who wants to mishmash all of it is better off indexing, because it is exactly the average of all the market participants.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You average out those four kinds of market participants, that’s the index.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You’re better off doing that.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you say – How do I make a business out of it? – In the end, you have to have people with a like- minded approach who stick with you.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The difficult thing about this line of work is that you have to be a bit contrarian in terms of human nature.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You’ve got to have some element of a mutated genome to think you are right because logic and facts say so, not because anybody else agrees or disagrees with you.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That requires a different kind of psychology.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Some people fit it, if you decide you don’t, don’t even try.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You also have to have people who believe in that to be along with you.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Therefore, you cannot say – I want to have the biggest fund, have this AUM. – It doesn’t happen that way.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You get what you deserve in the end.

speaker: Audience
text: When you are underwriting an investment, how do you ensure you have an adequate margin of safety and downside protection?

speaker: Li Lu
text: Where do you see the margin of safety, what have I learned in the last 10 years and how do I keep engaged this far, and structural changes between the U.S. and Chinese markets?

speaker: Li Lu
text: I don’t know what that means, but I will say something along those lines.

speaker: Li Lu
text: One of the distinguishing characteristics that separates a value investor from most other investors is the enormous attention paid to downside protection.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Investing is predicting the future, which is inherently unpredictable.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What you do is invest in the things you do know.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What you know could be limited.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Everybody starts with very limited known knowledge.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s how I started when I was in my 20s.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I didn’t know much.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I go with the things I know are there.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The balance sheet, obviously, as in Benjamin Graham’s work, because some things are easier to understand.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then I gradually progress from something simple to something less simple and more complex.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s a natural progression in terms of the circle of competence.

speaker: Li Lu
text: About circle of competence, one thing is to understand its edge.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The other is consciously to expand it gradually over time.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I always say, if you can compound your knowledge sustainably, eventually you can compound your capital as well.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That goes back to your question about what I’ve learned over 10 years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Every 10 years, I find I’ve learned so much that you’re almost somewhat a different person.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You want to have that renewed sense that, over a long period, if you do the right thing in the right way, it will be remarkable to find that you actually compound.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is another reason, I would say, if you want to choose to go to a win-win situation rather than zero-sum.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You actually will compound your ability and knowledge, and perhaps your health, too.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Maybe not quite, but you can at least prolong your productive span, your health span.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Maybe not lifespan, but your health span.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You keep engaged.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s interesting.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You know it’s helpful to society, and you’re not taking away from society.

speaker: Li Lu
text: With the zero-sum game, the trouble is that a lot of human nature goes to zero-sum, to the short term.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Whatever you learn today is useless tomorrow.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You don’t accumulate.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You rely more and more on the impersonal.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You get a bigger computer, and now you use AI.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You’ll be replaced at some point, so what is the value of that as a human?

speaker: Li Lu
text: Of course, I like the human in the loop.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I advocate learning, having an engaged and improved life over time, and compounding your knowledge as well as the capital of the people in the trusting way.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What my mentor, partner, and teacher Charlie Munger always said and advocated is that the highest order of relationship he could discover is a seamless web of deserved trust.

speaker: Li Lu
text: A seamless web of deserved trust!

speaker: Li Lu
text: There lies a whole philosophy of approaching life in a productive way that is win-win for society as well.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I recommend anyone starting your career to lean towards that way of life.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It could take years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It could be slow, but slowly and surely you will get to where you deserve to go.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is a better way of living.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Some people have a little more luck than others along the way.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Our life, success, and failure are sometimes a combination of lucky or unlucky breaks in life.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We’ve had a fair share of all of it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I, for one, never felt our record was completely our genius or anything.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We’ve got so many lucky breaks along the way.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But if you choose the right partners, the right approach, the right people to bet on, and the right things to do, over time it’s remarkable how compound returns work.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The basic idea of compounding is that you don’t lose what you already have.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s a profound idea.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You don’t lose what you already have, including your knowledge, your trusting relationships, your wisdom, and even your health.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Those are amazingly powerful things to have in life.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In that regard, I think structurally the U.S. and China are the same.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In fact, that’s the structure of humanity.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That doesn’t necessarily answer your question, I’m sure.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There are always changes in life.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is one constant we’re always going to have to deal with.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You will always have your share of luck and unluck, and your share of great opportunities, no matter which way you naturally lean.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Finding something you naturally lean towards and building on it over time in a compounded and cumulative fashion is just a better way of living a productive life.
